title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates SRE standards for service level objectives (SLOs), error budget policy and tooling, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review requirements, operational tooling expectations, and runbook templates. It is intended as the canonical reference for on-call engineers, service owners, and product teams to align reliability goals and operational practices across Redwood Inference.

Scope
- Services covered: inference-api, routing-service, kv-cache, batcher, telemetry-proxy
- Applies to: hosted API production clusters, Dedicated control plane, and Private control-plane deployments where SRE support is provided

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles
- Measure user-facing indicators (availability, latency at a client-visible percentile, correctness where applicable).
- Define one primary availability SLO and one latency SLO per customer-facing route/service.
- Keep SLO counts small and business-aligned; prefer conservative targets that reflect user expectations.

Required SLOs (examples)
- inference-api (public API)
  - Availability: 99.95% successful responses (2xx) per 30d window
  - Latency: p95 < 200ms for small requests (<= 512 tokens) per 30d window
- routing-service
  - Availability: 99.99% per 30d window
  - Tail latency: p99 < 50ms per 30d window
- kv-cache
  - Availability: 99.9% per 30d window
  - Hit rate: >= 85% per 30d window

SLO Definitions and Implementation Notes
- SLO windows: default rolling 30-day window. Quarterly reviews may add 7d/90d views for trend analysis.
- Error classification: Only count user-impacting errors. Internal 5xx that are retried transparently by the client should be excluded if end-to-end success is preserved. Document exclusions per service in its SLO definition doc.
- Measurement sources: Prometheus metrics exported by service (http_request_total, http_request_duration_seconds_bucket, http_response_success_total), with synthetic checks (Grafana Synthetic or k6) for external verification.

Error Budget Policy
- Error budget = (1 - SLO_target) * window. We track burn rate and remaining minutes per service.
- Response tiers (rolling 7-day burn rate unless noted):
  - Normal (burn rate <= 1): Proceed with normal release cadence.
  - Elevated (burn rate > 1 and <= 5): Pause feature rollouts that increase risk; increase monitoring cadence to hourly. Notify product and engineering manager.
  - Critical (burn rate > 5): Halt non-critical releases, engage incident response, and run mitigation/rollback. Schedule a post-incident review within 5 business days.

Escalation and Communication
- Alerts are routed to PagerDuty with the following escalation policy: primary -> secondary -> oncall-manager. For critical burns, a follow-up Slack channel is created (#sre-incident-<service>).
- Error budget spends and status are published weekly in the Reliability dashboard and to the service owner email list.

2) Capacity Planning

Goals
- Ensure capacity meets 99.95% latency and availability targets with headroom for traffic surges and scheduled maintenance.
- Reduce risk of capacity-induced incidents through proactive scaling, reservations for planned events, and chaos exercises.

Process
1. Monthly capacity review: each service owner provides 30/90/365 day traffic forecasts, utilization dashboards, and growth assumptions.
2. Quarterly capacity model refresh: update cost and capacity model inputs (instance types, GPU utilization, batching throughput, KV hit rates).
3. Pre-season planning: for major marketing campaigns or product launches, create a capacity runbook with reservation dates and rollback steps.

Capacity Targets and Headroom
- Target average CPU/GPU util at steady state: 60-70% (leave 30-40% headroom for burst).
- Autoscaling policies must maintain p95 latency target with 95% confidence on historical traffic patterns.
- Reserved capacity for black-swan: maintain a recovery bucket equivalent to 2 hours of peak traffic for critical services (inference-api).

Capacity Tooling
- Use the capacity planner spreadsheet (link: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planner-template) and BigQuery historical tables (redwood_prod_traffic.metrics).
- Alerts for saturation: PrometheusRule alerts for instance_cpu_utilization > 80% sustained for 5min, gpu_memory_util > 85% sustained for 2min, queue_depth > target for 3min.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Roadmap

Standard initiative types
- Reductions in blast radius (tiered routing, model fallback strategies)
- Cost vs reliability tradeoffs (quantization and batching profiles with guardrails)
- Observability improvements (trace context, span sampling, synthetic checks)
- Automated remediation (autoscaling improvements, instance replacement)

Quarterly example initiatives (Q3 2026)
- Initiative A: Autoscaler v2 rollout for batcher to improve cold-start handling (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
- Initiative B: Model-fallback catalog and policy for low-capacity regions (owner: eng-platform).
- Initiative C: End-to-end synthetic checks for core routes with error-injection coverage (owner: eng-sre).

Success criteria
- Measurable reduction in SEV rate attributable to the initiative (target: -30% SEVs over 90 days)
- Observable improvement in error budget burn frequency and reduced mean time to detect (MTTD)

4) Incident Review Standards

Post-incident expectations
- All incidents with P1/P0 severity must have a written postmortem within 5 business days with a follow-up 30-day action plan. P2 incidents above threshold (see incident-severity matrix) require a 10-business-day postmortem.
- Postmortems must include: timeline, impact description (users affected, duration), root cause analysis, corrective actions (owner + due date), and a quantified reliability metric improvement target.

Template (required sections)
1. Summary and impact
2. Timeline and detection
3. Root cause and contributing factors
4. Immediate mitigation and recovery steps
5. Long-term remediation plan
6. Action items with owners and due dates
7. Verification plan and metrics to confirm fix
8. Lessons learned and follow-ups

Review process
- Peer review by at least two SREs and the service owner.
- Postmortems for critical incidents are discussed at the next SRE retro and surfaced to product leadership.

5) Operational Tooling Expectations

Monitoring and Alerting
- Source of truth for service metrics: Prometheus -> Grafana dashboards. Dashboards must include: request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, system resource metrics (CPU/GPU/memory), queue depth, and SLO burn charts.
- Alerts must be actionable and include runbook links. Use severity labels: warning, critical, paging.

Tracing and Logs
- Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) must be enabled on customer-facing request paths. Trace context headers must be propagated through routing-service and batcher.
- Structured logs (JSON) with keys: service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, customer_id (nullable), error_code. Logs should be exported to Datadog and retained per security-and-compliance policy.

Testing and Chaos
- Integrate light-weight chaos checks in staging (pod eviction, disk pressure) and run quarterly chaos exercises on non-production clusters.
- Use canary releases with health gates measured against SLOs and synthetic checks.

6) Runbook Templates and Examples

Runbook conventions
- Title: service-name - short description
- PagerDuty escalation link and oncall owner
- Symptoms (what users see)
- Immediate mitigations (step-by-step)
- Diagnostics (metrics, queries, dashboards)
- Recovery steps and rollback criteria
- Post-incident actions and documentation links

Example: inference-api high error rate
- PagerDuty: inference-api-prod -> primary oncall
- Symptoms:
  1. error_rate (5xx) > 0.5% for 5 minutes
  2. Synthetics failing for /v1/generate endpoint
- Immediate mitigations:
  1. Check Grafana dashboard: inference-api/overview and SLO burn chart.
  2. If error spike coincides with recent deploy, `kubectl rollout status deployment/inference-api -n prod` and consider `kubectl rollout undo` for the last deployment if health fails.
  3. If backend model pool is saturated, increase pool size via autoscaler: `kubectl patch hpa inference-api --patch '{"spec":{"maxReplicas":<new>}}'` or trigger batcher autoscale script `./scripts/scale-batcher --increase 2`.
  4. For transient network errors, enable fallback routing: update Feature flag `routing-service.fallback_to_read_only=true` for the affected region.
- Diagnostics (queries)
  - Prometheus: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api",code!~"2.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api"}[5m]))`
  - Latency: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-api"}[5m])) by (le))`
- Recovery and rollback criteria:
  - Error rate back to < 0.2% for 10 minutes and SLO burn rate <= 1
  - All canary regions healthy for 15 minutes
- Post-incident actions:
  1. Create a postmortem and link to runbook.
  2. If caused by capacity, trigger capacity review and reserve additional capacity for the next 30 days.

Runbook for node GPU OOM (kv-cache)
- Symptoms: node reports OOM on GPU driver, pods evicted, increased 5xx for kv-cache
- Immediate steps:
  1. Move traffic away from node: cordon and drain `kubectl cordon <node>`; `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets`
  2. Relaunch a replacement node via infra self-healing script: `./infra/replace-node --node <node>` or open infra runbook if manual.
  3. If OOM due to model size, switch to a smaller quantized variant via feature flag `kv-cache.model_variant=quantized-4bit` (check compatibility first).

7) Roles and Ownership
- Service owner: accountable for SLOs, runbook maintenance, and capacity forecasts.
- SRE oncall: first responder for operational incidents and runbook execution.
- Eng Platform / Infra: responsible for autoscaler, instance pool health, and cluster-level mitigations.
- Product manager: notified when error budget reaches Elevated tier; involved in release pauses.

8) Governance and Reviews
- SLOs must be reviewed annually or when service changes significantly (e.g., new route, model change, change in SLA).
- Reliability initiatives must be prioritized in the roadmap with measurable success criteria.
- Runbooks must be validated in game-days at least twice a year.
